questions.prompt: The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes up to n in what time complexity?
questions.explanation: Marking multiples of each prime costs the harmonic-over-primes sum, which is O(n log log n). Testing each number individually for primality would be far slower.

questions.prompt: To test whether a single number n is prime by trial division, you only need to check divisors up to:
questions.explanation: If n has a factor larger than its square root, it must also have a matching factor smaller than the square root. So checking up to sqrt(n) is sufficient.

questions.prompt: Euclid's algorithm computes the greatest common divisor of two numbers by:

options.text: Repeatedly replacing the larger with the larger modulo the smaller

questions.explanation: gcd(a, b) equals gcd(b, a mod b), and the remainders shrink quickly until one becomes zero. It runs in O(log(min(a, b))) — logarithmic, not linear.

questions.prompt: The relationship between the GCD and LCM of two numbers a and b is:

options.text: gcd(a, b) + lcm(a, b) = a + b
gcd(a, b) x lcm(a, b) = a x b
gcd and lcm are always equal

questions.explanation: Their product equals the product of the numbers, so lcm can be computed as a / gcd(a, b) x b. Dividing first avoids overflow from the full product.

questions.prompt: Modular exponentiation (computing a^b mod m) by repeated squaring runs in:
questions.explanation: Squaring the base and halving the exponent needs only log b multiplications, each taken modulo m to keep numbers small. Naive repeated multiplication would be O(b).

questions.prompt: Why is taking a running result modulo m at each step important in modular arithmetic?

options.text: It is required for the result to be positive
It keeps intermediate values small and prevents overflow

questions.explanation: Because (a x b) mod m = ((a mod m) x (b mod m)) mod m, reducing along the way gives the same answer while bounding the numbers. This is essential for large exponents and products.

questions.prompt: The number of trailing zeros in n factorial is determined by counting factors of:

options.text: 5, since factors of 2 are always more plentiful

questions.explanation: A trailing zero comes from a factor of 10 = 2 x 5, and factors of 2 are far more common, so the count of 5s is the bottleneck. Summing floor(n/5) + floor(n/25) + ... gives the answer.

questions.prompt: Two numbers are said to be coprime (relatively prime) when:
questions.explanation: Coprimality means they share no common factor beyond 1, though neither need be prime itself — for example 8 and 9. It is central to modular inverses and the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

questions.prompt: The sum of the first n natural numbers, 1 + 2 + ... + n, equals:
questions.explanation: Pairing terms from the ends gives n/2 pairs each summing to n + 1, so the total is n(n + 1)/2. This closed form replaces an O(n) loop with an O(1) computation.

questions.prompt: Which structure efficiently supports many GCD-based range queries on a static array?

options.text: A sparse table, since GCD is idempotent and associative

questions.explanation: GCD, like min and max, is idempotent, so overlapping ranges can be combined, letting a sparse table answer each query in O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing. A segment tree also works but is slower per query.
